introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education (GCE) Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 2 (0790), Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are required to answer FOUR (04) questions, chosen from the three Sections imperatively.

Each essay question shall be marked according to the following criteria:
- An introduction: 5 marks
- A thesis: 7 marks
- An antithesis: 6 marks
- A synthesis: 3 marks
- A conclusion: 4 marks

Each question carries 25 marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : la page de garde dit « answer FOUR (04) questions, chosen from the three Sections imperatively » (quatre questions au total, prises dans les trois sections, donc au moins une par section). `regles_choix` porte le minimum, une règle `parmi 1 sur 2` par section (Section One : questions 1-2 ; Section Two : questions 3-4 ; Section Three : questions 5-6) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. Le sujet imprime « Sub Section Two: Text on African Philosophy » au-dessus de la question 6 mais aucun intitulé « Sub Section One » au-dessus de la question 5 (texte de Descartes) : la Section Three est comptée comme une seule section de deux questions ; le sujet ne dit pas si un candidat peut traiter les questions 5 et 6 à la fois.

Points : chaque question est imprimée « 25 marks » (4 x 25 = 100). Les critères de la page de garde (introduction 5, thèse 7, antithèse 6, synthèse 3, conclusion 4 = 25) s'appliquent aux dissertations (questions 1 à 4) ; les questions de textes (5 et 6) ont leurs points par sous-question (5 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 25 pour chacune) : aucun écart de somme constaté, aucun point corrigé.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les auteurs et positions cités sont ceux de l'histoire de la philosophie établie, sans citation littérale, sans numéro de page et sans date hormis des repères généraux sûrs ; à faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

Sujet scanné (3 pages) avec filigrane gcerevision.com sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Philosophy 2, Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture), code 0790, JUNE 2022, trois heures.

Q4 : la question (« Do you agree? ») demande une prise de position ; le corrigé conclut sur un accord partiel en exposant les positions et leurs raisons, sans parti pris partisan. Positions attribuées à Nkrumah et Nyerere (défense du parti unique et de l'unité nationale), à Wiredu (démocratie consensuelle sans parti) et à Gyekye (consultation et contrôle du pouvoir des chefs) : grandes lignes sûres, aucune citation littérale, aucun titre d'ouvrage, aucune date. Les exemples d'élections truquées, de coups d'État et de changements de pouvoir pacifiques sont volontairement généraux (aucun pays nommé).

questions.enonce_markdown:
In African political thought, democracy is still an illusion. Do you agree?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction (5 marks).** Democracy, in its modern sense, means government by the people through free and fair elections, equality before the law, respect for rights and the accountability of rulers. African political thought has dealt with it in two ways: by describing the democratic elements of traditional societies, and by judging the political systems built after independence. To say that democracy is "still an illusion" in this thought is to say that it exists in words and in constitutions but not in reality. The problem is whether this judgement is fair, or whether it ignores real achievements and the ways democracy has been adapted.

**Thesis: democracy is largely an illusion (7 marks).**
- *Disappointment after independence.* Many early leaders argued that multi-party competition would divide fragile new states along ethnic lines. Nkrumah and others defended strong single-party rule, and Nyerere presented the one-party state as an extension of traditional discussion among equals. In practice, single-party regimes and military coups replaced pluralism in a large part of the continent, and power was concentrated in a president and a small elite.
- *Form without substance.* Since the 1990s multi-party elections have returned almost everywhere, but critics point to rigged or contested elections, control of the media and of the courts, the manipulation of constitutions to remove term limits, patronage and corruption. Voting then takes place, but voters cannot remove the rulers: democracy is formal.
- *Ethnicity and poverty.* Where political parties follow ethnic lines and where most citizens depend on the state or on patrons for a living, votes are exchanged for favours and not cast on programmes. Political thinkers also argue that democracy imported as a ready-made Western model, without roots in local institutions, remains foreign to the people.

**Antithesis: democracy is not merely an illusion (6 marks).**
- *Traditional roots.* Philosophers such as Kwasi Wiredu and Kwame Gyekye argue that many African societies practised government by discussion and consensus, with councils of elders, checks on chiefs (a chief could be advised, resisted or removed) and the rule that decisions must carry the people with them. Wiredu proposed consensual, non-party democracy as an African contribution. This shows that democratic values are not alien to Africa.
- *Real progress.* Several states have seen peaceful changes of government after elections, independent courts, a lively press and active civil society, and citizens have forced leaders out or stopped attempts to cling to power by peaceful protest. Democracy is therefore a living practice in some countries, not only a word.
- *Democracy is a process.* Even old democracies have exclusions and inequalities; the fact that its ideals are not fully achieved does not make them illusory. Judging Africa against a perfect model is unfair, and the ideal itself is what citizens use to criticise their rulers.

**Synthesis (3 marks).** The judgement is true of the many regimes where elections are controlled and power is personal; it is false as a general statement on Africa. Democracy is better described as an unfinished and contested project than as an illusion: its institutions are fragile, but its values are widely claimed and fought for.

**Conclusion (4 marks).** I partly agree. Where democracy is reduced to the ritual of elections, with no accountability or real choice, it is indeed an illusion. But African political thought also shows that democratic ideas have local roots, that real gains exist, and that the weakness of democracy comes largely from particular conditions (ethnic politics, poverty, personal rule) which can be changed. The best-supported view is that democracy in Africa is incomplete rather than illusory, and that its consolidation depends on strong institutions, civic education and political forms that draw on both African and universal traditions.
